passages.title: The New Dog
sentences: A new dog came to the park.
He stood by the gate all alone.
His tail was down.
Pixel saw him.
Pixel ran over with his red ball.
He dropped it at the new dog's feet.
The new dog wagged his tail.
Then the two dogs ran and played until dark.
Sam smiled. "Pixel made a friend," he said.

passages.title: The Lion and the Mouse
sentences: A lion was asleep in the sun.
A small mouse ran across his paw and woke him.
The lion trapped the mouse under his big paw.
"Please let me go," said the mouse. "One day, I may help you."
The lion laughed at the idea of a tiny mouse helping a lion.
But he lifted his paw and let the mouse go.
Days later, the lion got caught in a rope net.
He pulled hard, but the ropes held him tight.
The mouse heard him roar and ran to help.
She chewed through the ropes, one by one.
Soon the lion was free.
"Thank you, little friend," said the lion.
After that, the lion and the mouse were friends.

credit.title: The Lion and the Mouse
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: The Bundle of Sticks
sentences: A farmer had three children who argued all the time.
One day, he gave them a bundle of sticks tied with a string.
"Try to break this bundle," he said.
Each child pushed and pulled, but the bundle stayed in one piece.
Then the farmer untied the string.
He gave each child one stick.
"Now try," he said.
Each stick broke with a loud snap.
"When you help each other, you are strong, like the bundle," said the farmer.
"When you argue, you are weak, like one stick."

credit.title: The Bundle of Sticks
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Maya Reads Out Loud
sentences: Every Friday, Ms. Ortiz's class had a share time.
This week, Maya signed up to read her new comic out loud.
She was quiet in class and liked to sit at the back.
When her name was called, her face got hot.
Her hands shook as she held the paper.
For a second, she wanted to sit back down.
Then she looked at Sam, who gave her a thumbs-up.
Maya took a deep breath and began to read.
Her voice was soft at first, but it got stronger with each page.
When she read the funny part, the class laughed.
At the end, everyone clapped.
Maya sat down with a small smile.
Later, Ms. Ortiz said, "That took courage, Maya."

passages.title: The North Wind and the Sun
sentences: The North Wind and the Sun had an argument.
Each one said, "I am the strongest."
Just then, a man walked down the road in a warm coat.
"Let's have a contest," said the Sun.
"Whoever can get the coat off that man is the strongest."
The Wind went first.
He blew a cold, hard blast at the man.
But the harder he blew, the tighter the man held his coat.
At last, the Wind stopped.
Then the Sun came out from behind a cloud.
She shone warm and gentle on the man.
Soon the man wiped his forehead.
He took off his coat and sat down in the shade of a tree.
The Sun won the contest.

credit.title: The North Wind and the Sun
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

steps.say: The question asks about kindness. So I look for kind acts in the story.
The lion was kind first. He lifted his paw and let the mouse go.
Later, the mouse was kind. She chewed through the ropes and set the lion free.
The lion's kind act came back to him as help from the mouse.
So the story says a kind act can come back to you.
